near_duplicate_resolution.original_overlap: Both original items asked the nurse to interpret a markedly elevated A1C against usual adult glycemic goals.
near_duplicate_resolution.resolution: Retain the richer A1C interpretation/limitations construct in V2-Q1468 and rebuild V2-Q0239 into recognition and initial treatment of hypoglycemia.

semantic_correction.stem: A client with diabetes who uses insulin becomes shaky and diaphoretic. Capillary glucose is 52 mg/dL. The client is awake, follows commands, and can swallow safely. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.A: Give oral glucose or another fast-acting carbohydrate that contains glucose.
options.B: Administer glucagon immediately even though the client is awake and able to swallow.
options.C: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before giving any carbohydrate treatment.
options.D: Give a high-fat snack as the initial treatment to slow absorption and prevent recurrence.

semantic_correction.rationale: The ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 define glucose below 54 mg/dL as level 2 hypoglycemia, which requires immediate action. For a conscious individual with glucose below 70 mg/dL, glucose is the preferred treatment, although another carbohydrate containing glucose may be used. The client is awake and can swallow, so oral glucose or another fast-acting glucose-containing carbohydrate is the best first action. Glucagon is used when the person cannot or will not consume carbohydrate by mouth. Waiting 15 minutes before initial treatment delays indicated care; the 15-minute interval is used to reassess after treatment. Foods or beverages high in fat or protein should not be used for initial treatment because they can delay the glycemic response.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Recognize level 2 hypoglycemia in an awake client who can swallow and initiate prompt oral glucose treatment before reassessing the glucose response.
semantic_correction.source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: resolved semantic near-duplication with V2-Q1468 by replacing the original elevated-A1C interpretation item with an entry-level hypoglycemia recognition and immediate-treatment construct sourced to ADA 2026; all options were rebuilt and re-audited.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original V2-Q0239 and V2-Q1468 both tested interpretation of a markedly elevated A1C. V2-Q0239 was rebuilt into an acute hypoglycemia recognition/treatment item to add distinct clinically meaningful coverage.
audit_findings_append.source_authority: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p. 13 — recognize changes and intervene; monitor diagnostic testing and intervene

option_audit.A: Correct. The client is conscious, can swallow, and has glucose well below 70 mg/dL; ADA recommends glucose as the preferred treatment.
option_audit.B: Plausible emergency therapy for hypoglycemia, but glucagon is not the best first action when the client is conscious and can safely take oral carbohydrate.
option_audit.C: Plausible because ADA uses a 15-minute reassessment interval, but that interval follows initial treatment rather than preceding it.
option_audit.D: Plausible as a later snack strategy, but ADA advises against high-fat/high-protein foods or beverages for initial hypoglycemia treatment because they may delay the glycemic response.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. The stem explicitly establishes that the client is conscious and can swallow, making oral glucose the source-supported first treatment while eliminating glucagon as the preferred initial route.

cueing_check.note: All options are plausible treatment-sequence decisions; the correct answer is not the longest and no mechanical padding was used.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: The item requires the entry-level RN to recognize an abnormal glucose result and intervene promptly, directly matching Reduction of Risk Potential activity statements.
